extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (attorneys and agents), USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline staff, and disciplinary counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural rules, and sanctioning criteria governing discipline of practitioners before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. Part 11, including practitioner duties to clients, cooperation with OED, service/answer rules, burden of proof, and factors for sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to act with reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner 'shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure includes not filing required responses (e.g., to an Office action or restriction requirement), allowing an application to become abandoned without client knowledge/consent, and failing to take adequate steps to revive an abandoned application. Case examples: failure to respond to restriction requirement and allowance of abandonment supported violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to reasonably consult with client about means (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall 'reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client’s objectives are to be accomplished.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation shown by failure to consult about status or strategy for responding to Office communications (e.g., not discussing how to respond to a restriction requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall 'keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes forwarding Office communications such as Notices of Abandonment and advising client promptly of important developments. Repeated unresponsiveness and failure to notify client of abandonment are cited as violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to explain matters to permit informed client decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall 'explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explaining consequences of failing to respond to Office actions, options for extension of time, petitions, and revival procedures. Failure to explain Notice of Abandonment and response options violates this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties upon termination of representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination, a practitioner shall take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client’s interests, such as giving reasonable notice, allowing time for employment of other counsel, surrendering papers/property, and refunding any advance payment of fee or expense that has not been earned or incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of violation: failing to refund unearned advance fees, not providing client files to successor counsel, and failing to withdraw or otherwise effectuate termination in a way that protects client interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative misconduct: telling a client a response was filed when it was not, or misrepresenting knowledge of abandonment. Such misrepresentations are aggravating and support severe discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate with OED and respond to lawful demands (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation of any matter before it, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED may issue Requests for Information and Evidence (RFI) under 37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)(ii); practitioners have an ethical obligation to respond. Failure to respond to RFIs or Lack of Response letters, despite receipt or notice, is a violation and can be an aggravating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes ignoring disciplinary proceedings, not participating in investigations, and other conduct that undermines the disciplinary process; such conduct supports severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered practitioner contact/noticing requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered practitioners must notify the OED Director of the postal address for the practitioner’s office, up to three email addresses where the practitioner receives email, and a business telephone number, and must provide written notice of any address change within 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must maintain current contact information independently of customer numbers; failure to do so can complicate service, but OED may still effect service by other means (e.g., mail to other addresses, publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of complaint and publication alternative (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must attempt service (e.g., certified mail) per § 11.35(a)(2); if service cannot be confirmed, notice by publication in the Official Gazette (two consecutive weeks) is authorized under § 11.35(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication starts a 30-day answer period from the date of the second notice; practitioners must be aware that publication is an authorized substitute for personal service when service attempts fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to timely file an answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to answer (or seek extension/late answer permission) after proper notice can result in default, where admitted facts support findings of rule violations and entry of sanctions (including exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by 'clear and convincing evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence is between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt; evidence must produce a firm belief or conviction as to the truth. Case citations and judicial definitions (e.g., Addington v. Texas) are used to explicate the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in determining sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations require consideration of: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply these four factors along with prior USPTO decisions. The decision cites specific cases and the ABA Standards as source material for applying the factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of legal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of legal discipline is to protect the public and the administration of justice, not to punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions are calibrated to protect clients and the integrity of the profession; this purpose informs selection of penalties such as suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA STANDARDS § 9.22 illustrations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include, inter alia: a dishonest or selfish motive; a pattern of misconduct; multiple violations; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding by intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders; refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct; substantial experience in practice; and indifference to making restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these factors to increase sanction severity. Examples: misrepresenting actions to conceal neglect (dishonest motive); repeated failures to communicate/respond (pattern); failure to answer complaint or to respond to OED (bad faith obstruction); not refunding unearned fees (indifference to restitution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA STANDARDS § 9.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors include, for example, absence of a prior disciplinary record and other circumstances that may justify reduced discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision found only 'absence of a prior disciplinary record' as present and afforded it little weight given the gravity/pattern of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions available and reinstatement eligibility (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions can include exclusion from practice before the USPTO; an excluded practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of the exclusion, subject to compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion is a severe sanction reserved where duties were knowingly/ intentionally violated and significant actual/potential injury occurred. Reinstatement requires meeting regulatory conditions under § 11.58.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to issue and enforce RFIs (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: During an investigation, OED may request information and evidence from a practitioner by issuing an RFI pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RFIs are lawfully issued investigatory tools; practitioners are obliged to respond within the required time or request extensions. Approved examples show RFI served by certified mail and its non-response used as grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Model Rules and disciplinary precedent in interpreting USPTO Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Rules are fashioned on the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct; the USPTO looks to the Model Rules, Comments, Annotations, and disciplinary decisions (state and USPTO) for guidance in interpreting obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory history (78 Fed. Reg. 20180) and cited USPTO precedents inform application of rules and sanctions; practitioners should consult these sources when assessing conduct and defenses.
